claim: Somatic mutations in the estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) gene (ESR1), especially Y537S and D538G, have been linked to acquired resistance to endocrine therapies.
source: Somatic mutations in the estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) gene (ESR1), especially Y537S and D538G, have been linked to acquired resistance to endocrine therapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing this link.

claim: Cell-based studies demonstrated that Y537S and D538G mutants confer ERα constitutive activity and antiestrogen resistance.
source: Cell-based studies demonstrated that these mutants confer ERα constitutive activity and antiestrogen resistance and suggest that ligand-binding domain dysfunction leads to endocrine therapy resistance.
evidence: This claim references cell-based studies that have been conducted.

claim: Y537S and D538G mutant ERs recruit coactivator in the absence of hormone while their affinities for estrogen agonist (estradiol) and antagonist (4-hydroxytamoxifen) are reduced.
source: We show that these mutant ERs recruit coactivator in the absence of hormone while their affinities for estrogen agonist (estradiol) and antagonist (4-hydroxytamoxifen) are reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Y537S and D538G mutations confer antiestrogen resistance by altering the conformational dynamics of the loop connecting Helix 11 and Helix 12 in the ligand-binding domain of ERα.
source: Further, they confer antiestrogen resistance by altering the conformational dynamics of the loop connecting Helix 11 and Helix 12 in the ligand-binding domain of ERα, which leads to a stabilized agonist state and an altered antagonist state that resists inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and biophysical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ERα is a ligand-activated nuclear hormone receptor and a major regulator of cell growth, survival, and metastasis in a large fraction of breast cancers.
source: The estrogen receptor α (ERα) is a ligand-activated nuclear hormone receptor and a major regulator of cell growth, survival, and metastasis in a large fraction of breast cancers.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ERα.

claim: Inhibiting the action of ERα with selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) or selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs), or reducing endogenous estrogen levels with aromatase inhibitors (AI), are effective treatments for many breast cancers.
source: Inhibiting the action of ERα with selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) or selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs), or reducing endogenous estrogen levels with aromatase inhibitors (AI), are effective treatments for many of these breast cancers (Strasser-Weippl and Goss, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The majority of metastatic breast cancers that initially respond to endocrine therapies become refractory despite continued expression of ERα.
source: Unfortunately, despite continued expression of ERα, the majority of metastatic breast cancers that initially respond to endocrine therapies become refractory.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about breast cancer treatment outcomes.

claim: Approximately 25% of patients who previously received SERM/SERD/AI treatments for an average of five years presented with conserved somatic mutations that were not identified in primary (untreated) tumors.
source: Approximately 25% of patients who previously received SERM/SERD/AI treatments for an average of five years presented with conserved somatic mutations that were not identified in primary (untreated) tumors.
evidence: This claim is based on clinical data from prior studies.

claim: The most prevalent ERα point mutations were Y537S and D538G.
source: The most prevalent ERα point mutations were Y537S and D538G, while several others were identified at significantly reduced frequencies.
evidence: This claim is based on clinical data from prior studies.

claim: Breast cancer cell-based studies revealed that the Y537S and D538G mutations conferred hormone-independent activation of ERα and reduced the inhibitory potency and efficacy of clinically prescribed SERMs and SERDs.
source: Importantly, breast cancer cell-based studies revealed that the Y537S and D538G mutations conferred hormone-independent activation of ERα and reduced the inhibitory potency and efficacy of clinically prescribed SERMs and SERDs (Toy et al., 2013; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Carlson et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior cell-based studies.

claim: The constitutive activity and antagonist resistance of the Y537S and E380Q mutations were first described in cell models in 1996.
source: Notably, the constitutive activity and antagonist resistance of the Y537S and E380Q mutations were first described in cell models in 1996 (Weis et al., 1996), and shortly thereafter, the Y537N mutation was found in a clinical sample of metastatic breast cancer (Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Y537N mutation was found in a clinical sample of metastatic breast cancer shortly after 1996.
source: Notably, the constitutive activity and antagonist resistance of the Y537S and E380Q mutations were first described in cell models in 1996 (Weis et al., 1996), and shortly thereafter, the Y537N mutation was found in a clinical sample of metastatic breast cancer (Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The Y537S and D538G mutations occur at the N-terminus of Helix 12 (H12) in the ERα ligand-binding domain (LBD).
source: The Y537S and D538G mutations are especially interesting because they occur at the N-terminus of Helix 12 (H12) in the ERα ligand-binding domain (LBD).
evidence: This is a structural observation based on known ERα structure.

claim: ERα LBD is an α-helical bundle, with the C-terminal helix, H12, functioning as a key structural component of the activating function-2 (AF-2) cleft that governs the agonist or antagonist state of the receptor.
source: Structurally, ERα LBD is an α-helical bundle, with the C-terminal helix, H12, functioning as a key structural component of the activating function-2 (AF-2) cleft that governs the agonist or antagonist state of the receptor.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about ERα.

claim: In the agonist conformation (e.g. estradiol (E2)-bound), H12 covers the ligand-binding pocket, docking between Helices 3 (H3) and 11 (H11), thereby facilitating coactivator recruitment to the AF-2 cleft via canonical LXXLL coactivator sequence motifs.
source: In the agonist conformation (e.g. estradiol (E2)-bound), H12 covers the ligand-binding pocket, docking between Helices 3 (H3) and 11 (H11), thereby facilitating coactivator recruitment to the AF-2 cleft via canonical LXXLL coactivator sequence motifs.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about ERα agonist conformation.

claim: In the antagonist state (e.g.SERM-bound), H12 occupies the AF-2 cleft using its own LXXML sequence, thereby blocking coactivator recruitment and ERα action.
source: In contrast, in the antagonist state (e.g.SERM-bound), H12 occupies the AF-2 cleft using its own LXXML sequence, thereby blocking coactivator recruitment and ERα action.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about ERα antagonist conformation.

claim: The greatest conformational discrepancy between the apo and E2-bound D538G structures lies at Y537.
source: The greatest conformational discrepancy between the two structures lies at Y537, which, in the unliganded structure, adopts a more WT-E2 like conformation by orienting toward H3 in chain A, thus returning the φ and ψ angles of residues 537 and 538 into the α-helical region.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison of x-ray crystal structures.

claim: Y537 of chain B in apo D538G matches the solvent-exposed orientation of the D538G-E2 structure whereby the φ and ψ angles for 537 and 538 are outside of the α-helical region.
source: Y537 of chain B, however, matches the solvent-exposed orientation of the D538G-E2 structure whereby the φ and ψ angles for 537 and 538 are outside of the α-helical region.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the x-ray crystal structure.

claim: Based on the conformational asymmetry between the two monomers in apo-D538G ERα, Y537 can switch between the buried state observed in the WT-agonist structures and the solvent-exposed orientation of the D538G-E2 structure.
source: Based on this conformational asymmetry between the two monomers in apo-D538G ERα, Y537 can switch between the buried state observed in the WT-agonist structures and the solvent-exposed orientation of the D538G-E2 structure (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Apo D538G has lost some—but not all—of the conformational attributes of the E2-bound mutant, which is consistent with its modest level of constitutive activity.
source: Thus, apo D538G has lost some—but not all—of the conformational attributes of the E2-bound mutant, which is consistent with its modest level of constitutive activity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the structural data in the context of the functional data.

claim: MD simulations of the WT and the D538G mutant showed an increased flexibility of the H11-12 loop as a result of the D538G mutation, inducing the Y537 side chain to rotate toward the bulk solvent.
source: MD simulations of the WT and the D538G mutant showed an increased flexibility of the H11-12 loop as a result of the D538G mutation, inducing the Y537 side chain to rotate toward the bulk solvent (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rotation of Y537 shifts the backbone conformations of residues 535–537 to occupy regions of the Ramachandran plot that are similar to WT-E2 and distinct from apo-WT.
source: This rotation shifts the backbone conformations of residues 535–537 (Figure 6E) to occupy regions of the Ramachandran plot that are similar to WT-E2 and distinct from apo-WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The D538G mutation allows the H11-12 loop to adopt conformations similar to WT-E2, despite the absence of ligand.
source: These mutation-induced changes allow the H11-12 loop to adopt conformations similar to WT-E2, despite the absence of ligand.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the MD simulation data.

claim: The removal of the ligand (WT-E2 vs. apo WT) results in more exposed positions for the hydrophobic residues in the loop region, thus destabilizing the H11-12 loop.
source: Analysis of the averaged atomic density for residues 533–536 in the WT simulations reveals that the removal of the ligand (WT-E2 vs. apo WT, Figure 6C) results in more exposed positions for the hydrophobic residues in the loop region, thus destabilizing the H11-12 loop, while the D538G mutation allows the receptor to maintain side-chain positions buried more deeply into the protein surface (WT-E2 vs. apo D538G, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The D538G mutation allows the receptor to maintain side-chain positions buried more deeply into the protein surface.
source: Analysis of the averaged atomic density for residues 533–536 in the WT simulations reveals that the removal of the ligand (WT-E2 vs. apo WT, Figure 6C) results in more exposed positions for the hydrophobic residues in the loop region, thus destabilizing the H11-12 loop, while the D538G mutation allows the receptor to maintain side-chain positions buried more deeply into the protein surface (WT-E2 vs. apo D538G, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The optimized packing of the hydrophobic loop residues was additionally quantified by the decreased solvent exposure for the WT-E2 and apo D538G conformations compared to apo WT over the course of the entire simulation.
source: The optimized packing of the hydrophobic loop residues was additionally quantified by the decreased solvent exposure for the WT-E2 and apo D538G conformations compared to apo WT over the course of the entire simulation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All of the changes that result from replacing D538 with glycine are consistent with increased stability of the H11-12 loop in the mutant, which likely contributes to its constitutive activity.
source: All of the changes that result from replacing D538 with glycine are consistent with increased stability of the H11-12 loop in the mutant, which likely contributes to its constitutive activity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the MD simulation data in the context of the functional data.

claim: The H11-12 loop and H12 regions showed decreased dynamics (i.e. increased stability) for the Y537S and D538G mutants with TOT, which displayed t1/2 = 60 and 62 min, respectively, whereas the t1/2 for the WT was 18 min.
source: Interestingly, these regions showed decreased dynamics (i.e. increased stability) for the Y537S and D538G mutants, which displayed t1/2 = 60 and 62 min, respectively, whereas the t1/2 for the WT was 18 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental trypsin digestion data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The half-lives for the H11-12 loop and H12 with TOT were higher than apo proteins alone suggesting that TOT binds and increases the overall stability of the protein, although to a lesser extent than does E2.
source: These half-lives were higher than apo proteins alone suggesting that TOT binds and increases the overall stability of the protein (Figure 4A), although to a lesser extent than does E2.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the trypsin digestion data.

claim: Comparison of HDX profiles for TOT-bound WT and mutants revealed that the mutant proteins adopt alternate conformations in H11/12 regions relative to the WT complex.
source: Comparison of HDX profiles for TOT-bound WT and mutants revealed that the mutant proteins adopt alternate conformations in H11/12 regions relative to the WT complex (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental HDX-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The D538G-TOT structure was solved to 3.06 Å with four dimers in the ASU by molecular replacement.
source: However, the D538G-TOT structure was solved to 3.06 Å with four dimers in the ASU by molecular replacement.
evidence: This claim is supported by x-ray crystallography data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Significant conformational differences are observed between WT-TOT (PDB: 3ERT) and D538G-TOT structures, both in H12 and the H11-12 loop regions.
source: Significant conformational differences are observed between WT-TOT (PDB: 3ERT) and D538G-TOT structures, both in H12 and the H11-12 loop regions.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison of x-ray crystal structures.

claim: These differences help account for the reduced potency and efficacy of TOT toward the D538G mutant ERα in breast cancer reporter gene assays.
source: We believe that these differences help account for the reduced potency and efficacy of TOT toward the D538G mutant ERα in breast cancer reporter gene assays.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior cell-based assay data.

claim: In D538G-TOT, L536 is oriented toward solvent rather than docking into the well-defined leucine-binding pocket found in the WT-TOT structure, and P535 occupies the space previously occupied by the L536 of the WT.
source: In D538G-TOT, L536 is oriented toward solvent rather than docking into the well-defined leucine-binding pocket found in the WT-TOT structure, and P535 occupies the space previously occupied by the L536 of the WT (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the x-ray crystal structure.

claim: The largest conformational change in the D538G-TOT structure occurs in the H11-12 loop (residues 527–537), where instead of extruding toward solvent, the loop is packed toward the interior of the protein by 9.6 Å compared to the WT (V534 alpha carbon to alpha carbon).
source: The largest conformational change occurs in the H11-12 loop (residues 527–537). Instead of extruding toward solvent, the loop is packed toward the interior of the protein by 9.6 Å compared to the WT (V534 alphacarbon to alpha carbon) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the x-ray crystal structure.

claim: This conformational change in the H11-12 loop likely explains why trypsin displayed a reduced ability to cleave at this region in the D538G-TOT complex.
source: This conformational change likely explains why trypsin displayed a reduced ability to cleave at this region.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation connecting the structural data to the trypsin digestion data.

claim: The tertiary amine at the terminus of the TOT ligand is observed in several conformations in the complex with D538G ER rather than the single conformation present in the WT-TOT structure.
source: Additionally, the tertiary amine at the terminus of the TOT ligand is observed in several conformations in the complex with D538G ER rather than the single conformation present in the WT-TOT structure.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the x-ray crystal structure.

claim: The flexibility of a glycine at position 538 reduces the ability of an antagonist to influence the H11-12 loop and H12.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the flexibility of a glycine at position 538 reduces the ability of an antagonist to influence the H11-12 loop and H12.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The D538G mutant adopts an altered antagonist conformation that resists antagonism relative to the WT-TOT complex.
source: Together, these data reveal that the D538G mutant adopts an altered antagonist conformation that resists antagonism relative to the WT-TOT complex.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: During the MD simulation of Y537S with TOT, H12 of Y537S was found to lie within the AF-2 cleft in a perturbed conformation compared to the WT-TOT crystal structure, similar to that seen in the D538G-TOT crystal structure.
source: During the simulation, H12 of Y537S was found to lie within the AF-2 cleft in a perturbed conformation compared to the WT-TOT crystal structure, similar to that seen in the D538G-TOT crystal structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the Y537S-TOT MD simulation, L536 no longer packs well with the leucine binding site on H3 but reorients to face the solvent, and the rest of the motif is also pushed outward and even shifted toward the C-terminus along the axial direction of H12 by half a turn.
source: Specifically, L536 no longer packs well with the leucine binding site on H3 but reorients to face the solvent, and the rest of the motif is also pushed outward and even shifted toward the C-terminus along the axial direction of H12 by half a turn (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Y537S-TOT complex data show that conformational changes serve to reduce the inhibitory potency of the SERM relative to the WT ERα LBD.
source: Like the D538G-TOT complex, our data for the Y537S-TOT complex show that these conformational changes serve to reduce the inhibitory potency of the SERM relative to the WT ERα LBD.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the MD simulation data in the context of the functional data.

claim: Somatic mutations in the androgen receptor are a known mechanism of acquired hormone therapy resistance in prostate cancer.
source: While somatic mutations in the androgen receptor are a known mechanism of acquired hormone therapy resistance in prostate cancer, somatic mutations in ESR1 have only recently been identified as an important mechanism of acquired endocrine therapy resistance in breast cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about prostate cancer.

claim: Somatic mutations in ESR1 have only recently been identified as an important mechanism of acquired endocrine therapy resistance in breast cancer.
source: While somatic mutations in the androgen receptor are a known mechanism of acquired hormone therapy resistance in prostate cancer, somatic mutations in ESR1 have only recently been identified as an important mechanism of acquired endocrine therapy resistance in breast cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on recent research.

claim: Y537S and D538G are the two most common point mutations conferring hormone-independent activation and reduced SERM/SERD/AI inhibitory potency and likely efficacy.
source: Subsequent studies have established Y537S and D538G as the two most common point mutations conferring hormone-independent activation and reduced SERM/SERD/AI inhibitory potency and likely efficacy (Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The constitutive activity of Y537S and D538G mutant LBDs stems from their intrinsic ability to adopt a stable agonist conformation in the absence of hormone, thereby leading to enhanced recruitment of SRC3 coactivators and increased ERα transcriptional activity.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the constitutive activity conferred by the Y537S and D538G mutations stems from the intrinsic ability of the mutant receptors to adopt a stable agonist conformation in the absence of hormone, thereby leading to enhanced recruitment of SRC3 coactivators and increased ERα transcriptional activity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined biophysical and structural data.

claim: The pre-organized agonist state of the mutants contributes to a decreased affinity for hormone and especially for SERMs because the stabilized H12 agonist conformation restricts ligand access to the hormone-binding pocket.
source: This pre-organized agonist state contributes to a decreased affinity for hormone and especially for SERMs because the stabilized H12 agonist conformation restricts ligand access to the hormone-binding pocket.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined biophysical and structural data.

claim: SERM action is further reduced by an altered antagonist state of H12 in the mutants.
source: In addition to reduced ligand affinity, SERM action is further reduced by an altered antagonist state of H12.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined biophysical and structural data.

claim: Recruitment of coactivators in the breast cancer cell is not inhibited as efficiently for the Y537S and D538G mutants as for WT ERα.
source: Thus, recruitment of coactivators in the breast cancer cell is not inhibited as efficiently for the Y537S and D538G mutants as for WT ERα.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined biophysical and structural data.

claim: The H11-12 loop plays an important and previously unrecognized role in regulating the behavior of H12, an essential molecular switch that is allosterically controlled by ligand.
source: In this regard, our data show that the H11-12 loop plays an important and previously unrecognized role in regulating the behavior of H12, an essential molecular switch that is allosterically controlled by ligand, which determines the differential ability of the ERα AF-2 to recruit coactivators and corepressors.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Antagonists with improved inhibitory potency will increase the dynamic character of mutant H12, an already appreciated aspect of SERD action.
source: Therefore, antagonists with improved inhibitory potency will increase the dynamic character of mutant H12, an already appreciated aspect of SERD action (Pike et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the data and prior knowledge about SERD action.

claim: Fulvestrant (a SERD, known to disorder H12) was the only molecule which could completely ablate the transcriptional activity of the Y537S and D538G mutants in breast cancer cells while TOT (a SERM) could not.
source: Additionally, our work provides a biophysical hypothesis for why fulvestrant (a SERD, known to disorder H12) was the only molecule which could completely ablate the transcriptional activity of the Y537S and D538G mutants in breast cancer cells while TOT (a SERM) could not (Toy et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on prior published cell-based studies.

claim: Newly developed mixed SERM/SERDs and SERDs with improved pharmacokinetics and oral bioavailability over fulvestrant, such as AZ9496, bazedoxifene, GDC910, and RAD1901, should be particularly effective against cancers expressing the Y537S and D538G ESR1 mutants.
source: Therefore, newly developed mixed SERM/SERDs and SERDs with improved pharmacokinetics and oral bioavailability over fulvestrant, such as AZ9496, bazedoxifene, GDC910, and RAD1901, should be particularly effective against cancers expressing the Y537S and D538G ESR1 mutants (De Savi et al., 2015; Garner et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2015; Wardell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the data and prior knowledge about these compounds.

claim: These compounds may prove invaluable for treating endocrine therapy-resistant ER+ breast cancers and also preventing or delaying the appearance of these somatic mutations in early-stage patients.
source: These compounds may prove invaluable for treating endocrine therapy-resistant ER+ breast cancers and also preventing or delaying the appearance of these somatic mutations in early-stage patients.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the potential clinical utility of these compounds.

claim: SRC3 was chosen for coactivator binding studies because of its abundance in breast cancer cells and high affinity for ERα.
source: SRC3 was chosen because of its abundance in breast cancer cells and high affinity for ERα (Liao et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.
